body.text: When a wooden fence needs a fresh finish, the choice often comes down to paint or stain, and the two are not simply different colours of the same product. They work in fundamentally different ways, and that difference is what determines how each one ages, particularly across Kitchener-Waterloo's freeze-thaw winters and humid summers. This guide compares how paint and stain perform over time on a fence, and why one tends to hold up better under the specific conditions this region sees.
How paint and stain actually work differently

Paint is a film-forming product. It sits on top of the wood surface, creating a continuous layer that seals the wood underneath and provides its colour and protection from that surface layer. Penetrating oil-based stain, by contrast, is designed to soak into the wood fibre itself rather than sit on top of it, carrying pigment and protective oils down into the grain. This is not a minor technical distinction; it is the reason the two products fail in completely different ways once they start to age, and it is the core reason stain tends to hold up better on exterior wood structures like fences over the long run.
Why paint eventually cracks and peels

Wood is not a static material. It expands and contracts with changes in temperature and moisture, swelling in humid summer conditions and contracting in dry, cold winter air. A paint film, because it sits on the surface as a separate layer, does not move with the wood underneath it in the same way. Over time, that mismatch causes the paint film to crack, and once cracks form, moisture gets underneath the film and accelerates peeling. This is a normal, expected failure mode for exterior paint on wood, not a sign of poor-quality product, and it is why painted fences eventually need scraping, sanding, and full repainting once the film starts to fail, a more labour-intensive process than most homeowners expect when they first choose paint for the lower upfront look.
Why stain fades instead of peeling

Because penetrating stain soaks into the wood rather than forming a separate surface film, it does not experience the same cracking and peeling failure mode as paint. Instead, stain gradually fades as UV exposure and weather break down the pigment and oils within the wood over time. This matters practically because a faded stain finish can usually be refreshed with cleaning and a new coat, without the scraping and aggressive surface prep that a peeling paint job requires. The wood underneath a well-maintained stained fence tends to stay in better condition over the years as well, since there is no trapped moisture issue building up under a failing film.
How this plays out across Southwestern Ontario's climate

This region's freeze-thaw cycles, where temperatures swing repeatedly above and below freezing through late fall, winter, and early spring, put more stress on exterior wood finishes than a milder, more stable climate would. Every freeze-thaw cycle is another round of the wood expanding and contracting, and for a rigid paint film, that repeated movement accelerates the cracking process. Stain, having soaked into the wood rather than sitting as a separate layer, moves with the wood more naturally through those cycles, which is a meaningful part of why stain generally holds up better here than in regions with more consistent year-round temperatures.

A painted fence that looks fine one winter can show significant peeling by the following spring once the freeze-thaw cycle has worked on existing cracks. Stain's gradual fading process does not carry the same risk of a sudden visible failure.
What redoing each finish actually involves

The practical difference between maintaining a stained fence and repainting one shows up clearly once a finish needs attention. A fence due for a stain refresh generally needs a thorough eco-friendly, plant-safe cleaning, appropriate sanding to open the grain again, and a new brush-applied coat, following the same clean, repair, sand and stain process used on decks. A fence with failing paint typically needs the old, cracked paint scraped or sanded off entirely before new paint can be applied, since painting over cracked or peeling paint locks in the existing failure and produces a worse result than starting from bare wood. That extra scraping and stripping step is often the most labour-intensive part of a repaint project, and it is a step stain maintenance simply does not require in the same way.
Appearance differences worth considering

Beyond durability, paint and stain also produce different looks, which is worth factoring into the decision alongside longevity. Paint offers a completely opaque, uniform colour and fully hides the wood grain, which some homeowners prefer for a clean, solid look or to match a specific colour scheme. Stain, even at the more opaque solid end of the spectrum, tends to retain at least some sense of the wood's texture and grain. If the priority is showcasing natural wood character, stain, particularly transparent or semi-transparent options, is the clearer choice. If a fully opaque, painted look is specifically what you want regardless of the maintenance trade-offs, that preference is worth weighing against the longer-term upkeep paint requires.
Cost considerations over the life of the fence

Restore My Deck's fence cleaning and staining and painting services fall within typical ranges of $800 to $1,200 for cleaning and $950 to $1,350 for staining or painting including prep, depending on the specific scope. Where the two diverge more is in the cost of upkeep over time. A stained fence generally needs a maintenance refresh every 2 to 4 years, a comparatively straightforward clean-and-recoat process. A painted fence, once the film begins failing, often requires a more involved and sometimes more costly scrape-and-repaint project to properly address peeling, which can make paint's long-term maintenance cost higher even if an initial paint job and an initial stain job are priced similarly.

That said, the right choice ultimately depends on your priorities: if a fully opaque, painted appearance matters more to you than long-term maintenance simplicity, that is a legitimate preference to weigh. For most homeowners focused on durability and lower long-term upkeep across Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge, Guelph, and the surrounding region, stain tends to be the more practical choice, particularly for fences that see direct exposure to sun, wind, and winter weather.

faq.q: Does stain or paint last longer on a fence in Kitchener-Waterloo?
faq.a: Stain generally holds up better over time in this climate, since it soaks into the wood and moves with it through freeze-thaw cycles rather than forming a rigid surface film that cracks and peels.

faq.q: Why does painted wood eventually peel?
faq.a: Paint sits on the wood surface as a film. As wood expands and contracts with temperature and moisture, the paint film cannot move with it in the same way, which eventually causes cracking and peeling.

faq.q: Is it more expensive to maintain a painted fence than a stained one?
faq.a: Often, yes, over the long run. A stained fence typically needs a straightforward clean-and-recoat refresh every 2 to 4 years, while a painted fence with failing paint usually needs more labour-intensive scraping before repainting.

faq.q: Can I switch my fence from paint to stain?
faq.a: It is possible but requires removing the existing paint down to bare wood first, since stain needs to penetrate the wood fibre directly. This is worth discussing as part of a quote for your specific fence.

faq.q: Does stain hide the wood grain like paint does?
faq.a: Not entirely, even at the more opaque solid end of the stain spectrum. If a fully opaque, uniform look is the priority regardless of maintenance trade-offs, paint may better suit that preference.

faq.q: What stain products does Restore My Deck use on fences?
faq.a: Premium penetrating oil-based stains, including Ready Seal and Penofin Verde, brush-applied rather than sprayed for deeper penetration into the wood fibre.
